system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 70-year-old woman with a history of coronary artery disease, prior CABG, GERD, and anxiety was admitted for two days of constant epigastric discomfort described as similar to her pre-bypass symptoms. Initial concern for cardiac ischemia was ruled out by normal EKGs, undetectable troponin levels on two occasions, and a normal exercise stress test. Her symptoms improved with pantoprazole, supporting a diagnosis of dyspepsia. She was found to have elevated blood pressure during admission, prompting an increase in lisinopril from 5mg to 10mg. Her anxiety, exacerbated by significant social stressors including her grandson’s uncertain living situation, was addressed with ongoing therapy and social work support. She remained stable throughout her stay, was discharged home on updated medications, and advised to follow up with her cardiologist and primary care provider.
problems: Dyspepsia and other specified disorders of function of stomach
Coronary atherosclerosis of unspecified type of vessel, native or graft

conversation_lines.text: I see. Is it worse at certain times of day?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, especially at night. I get so tired by then, even if I didn’t do much during the day. I still eat well, but I just feel drained.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And have you noticed any shortness of breath, chest pain, or swelling in your legs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No chest pain. I do have a little swelling in my legs, but that’s been there since my heart surgery years ago. I haven’t been short of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I also see you came in because of a cough and stomach upset after taking an antibiotic?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. I was seen last week for frequent urination. They said I might have a UTI and gave me Macrobid. I waited to get the brand name, but insurance didn’t cover it. So I took the generic that morning—and right after, my stomach hurt and I started coughing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’ve started you on some antibiotics here—vancomycin and ceftriaxone—for caution, but your urine culture came back with no growth, so we may adjust that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No growth? But I’ve been going to the bathroom so much. And cramps in my belly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the symptoms can still happen even without a clear infection. We’ll treat it with a different antibiotic—cipro—for seven days, just to be safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. But the weakness—I’ve been to so many doctors. They said I was low on vitamins, so I started B, D, and E. But I still feel awful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear your frustration. We checked your labs, and your white count was a bit high when you arrived, but it’s coming down. Your lactate was elevated, but you’re not septic, so we’re watching that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What does that mean—lactate?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a sign your body might be under stress. But yours is improving, and you’re not in danger. More importantly, we’re looking into the weakness. On exam, your proximal muscles—like your thighs and shoulders—are weaker than normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Proximal? What does that mean?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It means the muscles closest to your trunk—like when you stand up from a chair or lift your arms overhead. That’s where we see the most weakness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes! That’s exactly it. I’ve been needing help getting up. And my eyelid—my right one droops sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noticed that too—mild ptosis. We tested for myasthenia gravis, but the antibody test came back negative. That doesn’t rule it out completely, but it makes other causes more likely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what else could it be?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re considering a few things. You have a history of hypothyroidism, and your TSH is a bit high. That can cause muscle weakness. But your ESR and CRP are also elevated, which suggests inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So is it my thyroid?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. But sometimes inflammation can make the TSH look worse than it is. We’re increasing your levothyroxine from 100 to 112 mcg to help. But we also think you may have a type of muscle disorder that doesn’t show up on routine tests.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A muscle disorder? Like what?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not sure yet. It could be something called a cryptogenic myopathy—meaning we don’t know the cause. It’s not inflammatory, and your CK is normal, which is unusual. But your ESR is very high—90—which tells us something’s going on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I get worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right now, you’re stable. You’re able to walk with minimal help, and your breathing is fine. We don’t think this is urgent, but you do need a specialist. We’ve set up an appointment with neuromuscular neurology for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m just so tired all the time. And my husband’s been sick too—it’s been stressing me out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. Anxiety can make fatigue worse. We’ll continue to support you with that. You’re also on omeprazole—we’re lowering the dose from 40mg twice a day to 20mg, since you don’t have active reflux symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And the antibiotics—will I take them at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, ciprofloxacin twice a day for seven days. Finish the whole course, even if you feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better. The cough is gone, and my stomach feels okay. But I’m still weak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs this morning show your white count has dropped to normal. Lactate is gone. We’re stopping the IV antibiotics and keeping you on oral cipro.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What about the weakness? Will the thyroid medicine help?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It might, over time. But we still need to find the root cause. The neurology appointment will help. For now, you’re safe to go home tomorrow if you continue to improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your discharge is approved. You’ll go home today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m ready to go, but I’m still worried about the weakness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know. We’ve made the neurology appointment for next week. Keep taking your new thyroid dose, the cipro, and the lower omeprazole. Your PCP will check your thyroid levels in a few weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I feel worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your doctor. If you have trouble breathing or swallowing, come back right away. But you’re doing well. We’ll get answers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate your time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 70-year-old woman with a history of CAD s/p CABG, hypothyroidism, osteoporosis, and anxiety was admitted for generalized weakness, urinary frequency, and a nonproductive cough after starting a generic antibiotic. Initial evaluation revealed elevated WBC and lactate, but cultures were negative. She was treated with IV antibiotics initially, transitioned to oral ciprofloxacin for a presumed UTI. Her proximal muscle weakness, mild ptosis, and elevated inflammatory markers raised concern for a cryptogenic myopathy, though myasthenia gravis was not confirmed. Thyroid function was suboptimal, prompting an increase in levothyroxine from 100 to 112 mcg daily. She remained stable, with improving labs and no respiratory compromise. Discharged home with plans for outpatient neuromuscular neurology evaluation, continuation of ciprofloxacin, and follow-up on thyroid function.
